AfriScan · Botswana · Servitudes, road reserves and lease areas

Know what is changing inside your servitudes and lease areas in Botswana

We map structures, excavations, cleared ground and new tracks along power lines, road reserves and buried routes, and across mining lease and licence areas in Botswana. Each structure gets coordinates and its distance to your line or boundary, each stretch of the route gets an encroachment rating, and dated surveys show what is new. Satellite first, and a person reviews every result before you receive the PDF report and GIS files.

Send your route or boundary file See sample outputs

Our published sample is from Mozambique: the route of a high-pressure gas pipeline, with its 100 m band, on a Copernicus Sentinel-2 scene of 2 August 2026. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2026.

The rules behind the work BPC Act (Cap. 74:01) · Road-reserve wayleave permit · Mines and Minerals Act (Cap. 66:01) · Environmental Assessment Act · S.I. No. 71 of 2024 · IFC Performance Standard 5

Already on paper

The rules are on the ground

Botswana’s servitudes, road reserves and mining licences come with rules about what may stand on the land. Those rules only help if someone can see what is there, and when it arrived.

Servitude use

Power lines: grazing, not buildings

On the typical designs for BPC’s World Bank-financed 66 kV and 33 kV lines, the permanent right of way is 30 m and 15 m wide, and its permitted use is “Grazing. No cultivation or built infrastructure permitted.” (ESMF, Table 2-1). BPC’s technical-services desk takes requests about new developments that encroach on its servitudes (BPC).

Department of Roads

Road reserves: a wayleave for each service

Placing power, water or communication lines inside a road reserve needs an “Access Control to Road Reserve Space (Wayleave)” permit, and the A1 drawings sent with the application must show the utilities already in the reserve or close to it (gov.bw).

Mining licence

Mining: surface rights first

A mining licence application needs surface rights from the land authority or landowner, with a stamped sketch plan showing coordinates, environmental authorisation from the Department of Environmental Affairs and archaeological clearance (gov.bw). The Mines and Minerals (Amendment) Act, 2024, enacted in October 2025 and now in force, brought revised penalties, according to the Minister quoted by BOPA on 25 August 2026.

Where a new line, road or mine needs land, a dated record of what stands there, made before the route or footprint is fixed and repeated afterwards, is what later wayleave, compensation and community discussions go back to. See resettlement cut-off-date baselines and route and site selection.

What you receive

A dated register your servitude, land and GIS teams can use

  • Each structure listed with an ID, its distance to the line or boundary, its band, its chainage and its coordinates in WGS84 and in the route’s UTM zone.
  • Every 500 m rated high, medium or low for encroachment density, a count rule that tells your servitude officers which stretches to visit first. It is not a safety rating.
  • Cleared and cultivated ground inside a servitude, where the imagery shows it, and new tracks across it.
  • New and removed structures between dated surveys, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views.
  • A PDF report with maps, the segment table and the coordinate register, plus GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers that drop into the GIS your team already runs, and an interactive map file that opens in a browser.

How it works

From route file to reviewed register

  1. Send the route or boundary

    A line, road reserve, pipeline route or lease boundary in any common GIS format, with the widths or zones that matter. No file yet? Send pole, beacon or kilometre coordinates and we draw it with you.

  2. Satellite screening

    Structures, cleared ground and tracks are mapped along the whole route or area from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or imagery you already hold. Drone detail is added only for the stretches that need it, subject to the CAAB approvals and security clearances each job requires.

  3. A person reviews every result

    A reviewer confirms, corrects and adds to what the detection models and datasets propose. What the imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

  4. Report and GIS files

    The PDF report and layers go to the contacts you name. Re-surveys follow the schedule you agree with us.

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared and cultivated ground, excavations, tracks and vegetation. We do not identify, count or follow people, and whether a structure or a field is authorised is for you, the land authorities and the courts to decide. Our registers support your wayleave, compensation, legal and community processes; they do not replace any of them.

A person reviews every result

Building datasets and detection models propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds before anything is delivered.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled, never “real‑time”

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a notice of what changed after each one.

Confidential by default

Results go only to the contacts you name, registers carry no names, and sensitive sites are masked in every deliverable.

Satellite first, drones under S.I. No. 71 of 2024

Drones in Botswana, and why we start from satellite

Satellite and your own imagery. A survey starts from your route file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or orthophotos you already hold. No aircraft flies, so satellite-based servitude and right-of-way screening needs no drone permit and is available across Botswana, however long the line.

Drone detail. In Botswana every drone must be registered with the Civil Aviation Authority of Botswana (CAAB), and its owners and pilots go through security vetting. Commercial work needs a CAAB RPAS Operator Certificate, which is issued only to an operator with its principal place of business in Botswana, and an authorisation for each operation, including a security review of how the camera will be used. The 2024 regulations keep drones 50 m from people, vehicles and structures outside the operation’s control unless CAAB approves otherwise, and an earlier CAAB bye-law, still published on CAAB’s website, also restricts flights near power lines, parks, built-up areas and major roads.

Drone surveys are subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires. Afridrone is working towards the approvals Botswana requires, and every proposal with a drone element names the company that will fly it and its CAAB approvals, so your team can check them.

The Botswana drone-law guide

Who approves what, the operator certificate, the two sets of pilot-licence rules, the flight limits along a line, the older bye-law restrictions and an 11-point checklist for clients, with sources, last reviewed 27 September 2026.

Drone law in Botswana

For procurement and compliance teams

Citizen reservation, supplier registration and tenders

Public bodies, including ministries and parastatals, buy under the Public Procurement Act, 2021, in force since 14 April 2022. Section 76 reserves works, services and supplies procurement for citizens or citizen contractors, with reservation schemes prescribed for different areas, and accounting officers must satisfy themselves that no suitable citizen contractor is available before engaging others (PPRA, quoted by BOPA, 26 April 2023). Suppliers register with the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority on its Integrated Procurement Management System, by registration code and by citizen-ownership category: wholly citizen-owned, majority or minority citizen-owned, or wholly foreign-owned.

We respond to RFQs and tenders. Send the tender or RFQ number and any supplier or prequalification forms with your request, and tell us whether the procurement is reserved for citizen contractors. The proposal states which registrations are in place for your contract and which are being arranged. If your organisation buys through its own supplier portal, name it.

Frequently asked questions

Which servitude widths do you measure in Botswana?

The ones that apply to your line. The only widths we found published are the typical designs for BPC’s World Bank-financed 66 kV and 33 kV lines, with permanent rights of way of 30 m and 15 m, which the framework says “will be further defined” as the project is implemented (ESMF, May 2024). For 132, 220 and 400 kV lines, send the width per line or the servitude polygons from your GIS. Up to six widths can be reported in one survey.

Does a satellite survey need CAAB approval?

No aircraft is flown, so satellite-based servitude and right-of-way screening needs no drone permit and is available across Botswana. We found no Botswana law restricting the analysis of commercial satellite imagery; counsel should confirm it for your project. Drone detail, where you want it, is planned separately and is subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires.

Can you tell us whether a structure is lawful?

No. We map what stands where, and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether a structure on tribal land, state land or a freehold farm is allowed, or predates the servitude, is for you, the Land Board or other land authority and the courts to decide. The register gives them a dated, located list to work from.

Is the register a cadastral survey?

No. The Department of Surveys and Mapping regulates cadastral surveying and approves cadastral surveys for the registration of title under the Land Survey Act (Cap. 33:01) (Ministry of Lands and Agriculture). Our registers are monitoring and planning records built from imagery. They show your surveyor and your wayleave officers where to look.

Can you detect cable theft or vandalism?

No. Satellites cannot see theft, vandalism or people. We map land change, such as fresh digging, spoil, new tracks, cleared ground and new structures along a line or buried route, so that your patrols and land teams know where to look first.

Who sees our routes and the results?

Only the contacts you name. Registers describe structures, not people, and carry no names. We never publish maps of your assets or of the settlements around them without your written permission, and sensitive sites are masked in the deliverables.

Send the line, the road reserve or the lease boundary. We start from satellite.

Send the route or boundary (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the district and the widths that apply: the servitude width of each line, the road reserve, or your lease boundary and any buffer around it. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
